title: Cloth and season
heading: Warmth is woven, not cut
intro: One shape all year. What suits a robe to cold or warm months is the weave and the lining, not the cut {6:p.20}.

label.title: Summer Robe (Katabira) with Irises at Yatsuhashi
label.material: Plain-weave ramie with paste-resist dyeing, stencil-dyed dots (suri-bitta), hand-painted details...
label.insight: Made of ramie for summer. Druet writes that it is <q>the weaving (and whether there is lining or not)</q> that suits a kimono to cold or warm months {6:p.20}.

label.title: Unlined Kosode (Hitoe) with Grasses and Dewdrops
label.meta: Japan · Edo period · second half of the 18th–19th century
label.material: Resist-dyed plain-weave silk gauze (ro) embroidered with silk and metallic thread
label.insight: Unlined, and woven as gauze. In Druet's account of present-day practice, ro and sha arrive <q>while the hot and humid days of August linger</q> {6:p.20}.

label.title: Sashiko Kimono
label.material: Indigo-dyed plain-weave cotton, quilted and embroidered with white cotton thread
label.insight: A Japanese design study notes that silk often serves formal and outing wear, and cotton, wool or synthetics everyday wear {7:p.76}.

label.title: Obi with “Whose Sleeves?” (Tagasode) Pattern
label.meta: Japan · Edo period · first half of 19th century
label.material: Twill-weave silk with supplementary weft patterning and metallic thread
label.insight: Its record gives 414 × 63.5 cm. Today's formal fukuro or nagoya obi are <q>approximately thirty centimetres</q> wide, Becke notes {4:p.71}.

cards.title: The kimono year
body: Druet's account of present-day practice. She reads its steady presence in monthly magazines as <q>a guiding principle, not mandatory but strongly encouraged</q> {6:p.22}.
head: Kimono
Under-kimono
rows: Yukata, or sheer ro or sha {6:p.20}

cards.title: Ahead of the season
body: Druet calls it sakidori: dressing <q>to convey feelings towards a season that hasn't come yet</q> {6:p.27}. One guide advises a flower pattern <q>about one month ahead of the actual blossoming</q> {4:p.62}.
Motifs of a <q>past season</q> are a faux pas {6:p.27}.

cues.show: Look at the robes on this wall. Across the year, nothing about their cut changes. The sleeves keep their length. The skirt is never shortened.
What changes is the cloth. Three Japanese design researchers put it plainly: the shape is the same from formal wear to everyday wear. The fabric, and what is dyed or woven into it, decides the use.
Changing one wardrobe for the next has its own name, koromogae. Druet counts it among the care rituals, beside airing a whole collection at once.

Is summer kimono cool? A Japanese laboratory study dressed women in summer kimono in a hot room. The robe is full of openings: collar, cuffs, sleeve slits, hem. Even so, over the stomach the humidity passed ninety per cent. In one wearer's trials, silk stayed drier than polyester.
The season is also worn early. A summer robe may already carry the bellflower of autumn. Further along this wall, the pattern begins to say more than the month.

claims.text: Warmth or coolness comes from tailoring, weave and lining, not from the cut or length.
claims.quote: it is just the tailoring, the weaving (and whether there is lining or not) that makes a kimono appropriate for cold or warm months
claims.scope: Druet; general, present-day

claims.text: Seasonal change never alters the kimono's shape or sleeve length.
claims.quote: kimono fashion does not rely on changing the shape of the garment nor on having variation in the length of the sleeves
claims.scope: Druet; general

claims.text: The skirt part is never shortened.
claims.quote: The skirt part is always tailored as a long cylindrical wrap, and it is never shortened either
claims.scope: Druet; general

claims.text: The move into sheer ro or sha (or yukata) usually happens in the hot, humid days of August.
claims.quote: semi-transparent summer kimono made of ro (絽) or sha (紗) "breathable" weave, usually happens while the hot and humid days of August linger
claims.scope: Druet; present-day; August, not the whole summer (the sentence begins 'The transition into yukata ... or')

claims.text: The nagajuban changes by season: silk or polyester October to May, ro or sha June to September.
claims.quote: warm materials such as silk or polyester used from October to May, thinner fabrics such as ro or sha from June to September
claims.scope: Druet; general, present-day (note polyester)

claims.text: Nothing is worn under the cotton yukata.
claims.quote: and actually nothing underneath the cotton yukata
claims.scope: Druet; present-day

claims.text: Awase, the lined kimono, suits October until May.
claims.quote: with awase (袷 lined kimono), one can enjoy an outfit that would be appropriate from October until May
claims.scope: Druet; general statement on present-day practice

claims.text: Hitoe, the unlined kimono, is for the warm months from June to September.
claims.quote: it is the lightness of the fabric that is appreciated, especially during the warm months that spread from June to September
claims.scope: Druet; the sentence begins 'With hitoe (単衣 unlined kimono)'. Checked on the page text (extends v2 row 59).

claims.text: Seasonal dress is a guiding principle, not a rule.
claims.quote: a guiding principle, not mandatory but strongly encouraged
claims.scope: about seasonal kimono as presented in monthly magazines

claims.text: The rotation of the wardrobe is called koromogae, one of the care rituals.
claims.quote: the rotation of outfits inside one's wardrobe known as koromogae (衣替え)
claims.scope: Druet; described among 'care rituals', not a dated rule

claims.text: Mushi boshi: airing the whole collection at once, seasonally.
claims.quote: the seasonal airing out of one’s collection of outfits all at once, known as mushi boshi (虫干し)
claims.scope: Druet; care ritual

claims.text: The kimono's form is the same from formal to everyday wear; fabric and dyed or woven design decide its use.
claims.quote: キモノの形態は礼装から普段着まで共通であり，衣服としての用途は，布の材質および染織などの意匠によって決まる
claims.scope: Tr. "the form is common from formal to everyday wear; its use is decided by fabric and dyed or woven design". Maruyama, Tauchi and Kubo, summarising Ōtsuka 1972

claims.text: Silk is often used for formal to outing wear; cotton, wool and synthetics for everyday wear.
claims.quote: 礼装から外出着には絹が，普段着には木綿やウール，化学繊維などが用いられる場合が多い
claims.scope: Tr. "silk is often used for formal to outing wear; cotton, wool and synthetics for everyday wear". general; varies by period and region, the authors add. Not about this object.

claims.text: Fukuro and nagoya obi are about thirty centimetres wide.
claims.quote: These fukuro or nagoya obi are characterised by a width of approximately thirty centimetres
claims.scope: Becke, citing Kimura 2010, Ōkubo 2012; present-day formal obi. Not about this object.

claims.text: A kimono has many openings and looks cool in structure.
claims.quote: 和服はえり・そで口・ふり・身八つ口・すそ等の多くの開口部を有し，構造上からみても涼しげである
claims.scope: Tr. "wafuku has many openings such as collar, cuffs, furi, miyatsuguchi and hem, and is cool-looking in structure too". authors' statement; the study is titled for a hot environment (暑熱環境下)

claims.text: In summer kimono humidity above 90% arose at the upper abdomen: stuffiness turning to wetness.
claims.quote: 上腹部において90%を超える高い湿度が生じていることから判断して，蒸れから濡れの現象が起きている
claims.scope: Tr. "judging from humidity above 90% at the upper abdomen, stuffiness is turning to wetness". laboratory chamber, 3 women; summer kimono layers

claims.text: Humidity was highest in polyester and lowest in silk.
claims.quote: ポリエステルの着装が最も高く，逆に絹の着装が低いという結果が得られた
claims.scope: Tr. "polyester outfit highest, silk lowest". single subject for the material comparison

claims.text: Sakidori: conveying feelings toward a season that has not come yet.
claims.quote: sakidori (先取り) culture, which is to convey feelings towards a season that hasn't come yet
claims.scope: Druet; general statement

claims.text: One guide says to wear a flower pattern about one month ahead of the blossoming.
claims.quote: start wearing a specific flower pattern about one month ahead of the actual blossoming of the drawn flower
claims.scope: reported: Becke quoting Shimada 2017, a guide; advice, not observed practice

claims.text: Wearing hues or motifs of a past season is a faux pas.
claims.quote: dressing in hues or motifs that are of the passed / past season would be considered a major “fashion faux-pas”
claims.scope: Druet; general

claims.text: Unlined summer kimono often carry autumn plants such as kikyō (bellflower).
claims.quote: unlined summer kimono and obi, as they are often adorned with flowers and plants recognized as autumn markers, such as kikyō
claims.scope: Druet; sakidori

claims.text: Pattern signals formality, season and the wearer's gender, age and standing (turn to the next room).
claims.quote: personal attributes such as the wearer’s gender, age, social standing and taste
claims.scope: Becke, citing Dalby 2001: 164; general

dropped: A lined (awase) kosode on the wall: no Met record in the wishlist says 'lined'.
What ramie is and how the katabira differs from hitoe: no source read defines katabira or ramie.
Season of irises: no source ties the iris motif to a month.
Any fact about weaving or the loom in the stills: no source read describes it; the captions describe only the pictures.
The exact June/September hitoe and July-August usumono calendar used in many guides: only Druet's broader months were read.
The nagajuban photograph moved to room 7 (the family) to avoid showing it twice.
The weaving-room pictures: not rendered (cut to save time), so the room opens on the wall.
